title: Carillion: How Britain's Biggest Builder Ran Out of Money

scenes.say: On 15 January 2018, one of the British government's biggest contractors went into liquidation.

visual.text: Carillion goes into liquidation

scenes.say: It ran around 420 public-sector contracts. It employed around 43,000 people worldwide, around 18,000 to 19,000 of them in the UK.
It had liabilities of almost seven billion pounds. And it reportedly had just 29 million pounds of cash left.

visual.title: What it owed vs. what it had
visual.src: Company figures as reported, via Wikipedia

scenes.say: Four months later, two committees of MPs gave their verdict. Carillion's rise and spectacular fall, they wrote, was a story of recklessness, hubris and greed.

visual.text: Carillion's rise and spectacular fall was a story of recklessness, hubris and greed.
visual.by: Work and Pensions and BEIS Committees, 16 May 2018
visual.src: House of Commons committees report, May 2018

scenes.say: This is how a company that built hospitals, schools and railways ran out of money, and who was left to pay.

visual.text: How Britain's biggest builder ran out of money

scenes.say: Carillion was born in July 1999, when the construction group Tarmac split off its building business. Its headquarters were in Wolverhampton.

visual.text: Building an empire

scenes.say: From the start, it grew by buying. In 2006 it bought the builder Mowlem for around 350 million pounds.

visual.text: Buys Mowlem for about £350m

scenes.say: In 2008 came Alfred McAlpine, for 572 million. In 2011, the energy-services firm Eaga, for 306 million.
By 2016, Carillion's revenue was around 5.2 billion pounds a year.
It did everything from building roads and hospitals to maintaining prisons and serving school dinners. To the government, it looked like a safe pair of hands.
But the MPs' report described a very different business underneath.

visual.text: The dash for cash

scenes.say: They called its model a relentless dash for cash, driven by acquisitions, rising debt, expansion into new markets and exploitation of suppliers.

visual.text: Its business model was a relentless dash for cash, driven by acquisitions, rising debt, expansion into new markets and exploitation of suppliers.
visual.src: House of Commons committees report, May 2018

scenes.say: The numbers back that up. The House of Commons Library found that Carillion's debt rose more than fivefold, from 242 million pounds in December 2009 to around 1.3 billion by January 2018.
Over the same years, it kept paying shareholders: 554 million pounds in dividends between 2009 and 2016.
Between 2012 and 2016, the Library calculated, dividends were 63 million pounds more than the cash its operations actually generated.
So where did the cash come from? Partly from the people it owed.

visual.text: Where did the cash come from?

scenes.say: Carillion signed the government's Prompt Payment Code, yet it imposed standard payment terms of 120 days on its suppliers.
Suppliers who wanted their money sooner could use an early payment facility, but only by accepting less than they were owed.

visual.title: The early payment facility
items: Accepting less than they were owed

scenes.say: Rachel Reeves, then chair of the business committee, said Carillion's early payment facility ripped off their suppliers, forcing them to accept a cut in what they were owed.

visual.text: Carillion's early payment facility ripped off their suppliers, forcing them to accept a cut in what they were owed.
visual.by: Rachel Reeves MP, Chair, BEIS Committee, May 2018

scenes.say: On 10 July 2017, the cracks became public.

visual.text: 10 July 2017

scenes.say: In a trading update, Carillion announced a provision of 845 million pounds against its contracts: 375 million in the UK and 470 million overseas.
There would be no dividend that year. The chief executive, Richard Howson, stepped down, and Keith Cochrane took over as interim chief executive.

visual.title: The same day
items: Chief executive Richard Howson steps down
Keith Cochrane becomes interim chief executive

scenes.say: Investors ran. Over the announcement and the following two days, the shares lost 70 per cent of their value.

visual.label: Share value lost in three days

scenes.say: And yet, in the weeks after that warning, the government kept handing Carillion work.

visual.text: And yet, the contracts kept coming

scenes.say: The National Audit Office later counted four new central government contracts and three extensions, worth around 1.9 billion pounds, announced after the profit warning.
The bad news kept coming.

visual.text: The last six months

scenes.say: On 29 September 2017, Carillion reported losses of 1.15 billion pounds for the first half of the year, after a further 200-million-pound provision on its support services contracts.

visual.text: Half-year loss of £1.15bn

scenes.say: On 17 November, it warned it would breach its banking covenants, and the shares fell by more than half.

visual.text: Warns it will breach banking covenants

scenes.say: In early January 2018, Carillion asked the government for 223 million pounds to keep it going until April.
The Cabinet Office declined, deciding instead that Carillion should go into liquidation.
On 15 January 2018, Carillion went into compulsory liquidation. According to reports at the time, it would have run out of cash within days.

visual.text: 15 January 2018

scenes.say: The effects spread fast. Around 30,000 suppliers were owed roughly a billion pounds.

Work stopped on two hospitals being built under private finance deals: the new Royal Liverpool University Hospital and the Midland Metropolitan hospital near Birmingham were both hit, and Midland Metropolitan was already running well behind schedule.

visual.title: Hospital building work stopped
items: Midland Metropolitan University Hospital, near Birmingham (already running late)

scenes.say: The workforce paid first.

visual.text: Who paid

scenes.say: By June 2018, the National Audit Office reported that around 11,600 of Carillion's UK staff had found new work, about 2,300 had been made redundant, and around 3,000 were still working for the company in liquidation.
Pensioners were next. Carillion's UK pension schemes covered around 27,000 members, and about 2.6 billion pounds of liabilities passed to the Pension Protection Fund.

items: liabilities to the Pension Protection Fund

scenes.say: The MPs said the company's pension obligations had been treated with contempt.

visual.text: Long term obligations, such as adequately funding its pension schemes, were treated with contempt.
visual.src: House of Commons committees report, May 2018

scenes.say: And taxpayers paid too. The National Audit Office estimated a loss to the government of around 148 million pounds, and warned the figure was uncertain.

visual.label: Estimated loss to the government
visual.sub: Subject to a range of uncertainties

scenes.say: The MPs' report, published on 16 May 2018, spared almost no one.

visual.text: The verdict

scenes.say: It found Carillion's board both responsible and culpable for the failure, and pointed to a rotten corporate culture.

visual.text: Carillion's board are both responsible and culpable for the company's failure.
visual.src: House of Commons committees report, May 2018

scenes.say: It said the directors presented themselves as self-pitying victims of a maelstrom of coincidental and unforeseeable mishaps.

visual.text: They presented to us as self-pitying victims of a maelstrom of coincidental and unforeseeable mishaps.
visual.src: House of Commons committees report, May 2018

scenes.say: It said the auditor, KPMG, had been complacently signing off the directors' increasingly fantastical figures.

visual.text: ...complacently signing off the directors' increasingly fantastical figures.
visual.src: House of Commons committees report, May 2018

scenes.say: It said the Pensions Regulator had failed, and criticised the government for lacking the decisiveness or bravery to pursue the reforms they recommended.

visual.title: Also criticised
items: The Pensions Regulator: failed in its objectives
Government: lacked "the decisiveness or bravery" to pursue recommended reforms
visual.src: House of Commons committees report, May 2018

scenes.say: The regulators followed. In October 2023, the Financial Reporting Council fined KPMG a record 21 million pounds over its Carillion audit work.

visual.title: KPMG fined £21m
lines: !A record fine over Carillion audit work

scenes.say: In January 2026, the Financial Conduct Authority fined two former finance directors, Richard Adam and Zafar Khan, 232,800 and 138,900 pounds.
On 16 February 2026, it fined Richard Howson 237,700 pounds, finding he acted recklessly and was knowingly concerned in breaches by Carillion over misleading announcements to investors.

visual.title: Former CEO fined £237,700
lines: !"acted recklessly and was knowingly concerned in breaches by Carillion"

scenes.say: Carillion wasn't brought down by one bad contract. On the MPs' account, it was years of growth by acquisition, rising debt, generous dividends and suppliers paid late, held together by accounts that looked better than the cash.

visual.title: Not one bad contract
items: Accounts that looked better than the cash

scenes.say: The warning signs were in the public record all along. The question is who is reading them now.

visual.text: The warning signs were in the public record all along

scenes.say: If you want the next collapse told from the paperwork, subscribe. The sources for everything in this video are in the description.

visual.text: Subscribe for the next case file
visual.sub: All sources are in the description

summary: In January 2018, Carillion, one of the UK government's biggest contractors, collapsed with liabilities of almost £7 billion. Using the official reports, we trace how a company that built hospitals and railways ran out of money, and who paid for it.
